html:
Dutch Guiana was the Dutch colony of Surinam on the northeast coast of South America, now independent Suriname. The map shows it under this name in 1880 and 1900.

The Netherlands abolished slavery there in 1863, among the last European states to do so, and made the freed people work ten more years on the plantations under state supervision. When that ended in 1873, planters looked for new workers. Like British Guiana next door, the colony brought in contract labourers from British India from 1873, part of Indian indenture, and from 1890 from Java in the Dutch East Indies.

Their descendants, with the Creoles, Maroons and Indigenous peoples, make up Suriname's very mixed population today. Gold and balata rubber drew workers inland around 1900, and bauxite mining began after 1916. The colony gained self-rule in 1954 and independence in 1975.
